from a newsletter I subscribe to : 

> The annual compensation review cycle is wrapping up at Netflix. Starting 24 October, all staff will have 1:1 conversations with their manager and learn whether their compensation will change.
> 
> Netflix is preparing everyone to expect very low – or possibly no – raises this year. In an email to all staff, leadership shared a lot of context. It reads:
> 
>     “We’ve always had a different philosophy about compensation at Netflix, so we wanted to share more about (...) what has/hasn’t changed this year.
> 
>     We pay personal top of market (PTOM). For over a decade, our core philosophy has been to pay personal top of market so that we can attract the best performers. (...)
> 
>     This year we’ve invested in much more robust data to help us answer [questions on the personal top of market]. This includes salary data from companies we hire from or where people go after Netflix, input from candidates and information from employees who receive other offers.
> 
>     We have developed top of market reference ranges across different roles and levels. Again this is new for Netflix on many teams. Managers use these market reference ranges as an input to make decisions about compensation.
> 
>     Our ranges provide a starting point, but personal top of market is, well… personal. Our market reference ranges are broad, and intentionally so - they define a range for the role, and someone’s PTOM will sit somewhere within that range depending on their exact scope, impact, experience, performance trajectory etc.”
> 
> Netflix is introducing cost budgets for teams, which is new for the streaming provider. Team and organization leaders need to stay within their total cost budget.

Does Netflix/Uber/Meta also PIP for changing teams? 
In Amazon US, one has to be careful while changing teams that manager shouldn't know about it. If hiring manager informs current manager and then rejects the candidate, then candidate ends up in PIP Also, if someone leaves the team in Oct/Nov, the old teams usually gives lowest rating as candidate has already left the team. Then the next team will find it very difficult to save candidate from PIP. Therefore, team change has to be done in Mar/April after getting a good rating. Above details have nothing to do with performance. I have seen top notch performers getting PIPed and fired and having to leave USA because they couldn't hide their team change plan or did not make friends / did not hang out with their manager

In a managers meeting at Amazon our director chastized a new sr mgr for letting someone escape to another team who was about to get pip'ed.  He was told now he has to pip someone else to make the URA quota.  Nice.
A similar dynamic at Meta since they also have forced quota to Meets Most Expectations or below.  It may or may not result in a pip but often does.

Managers can always come up with something not up to par.
Meta does not PIP for changing teams.

Total interviews -10
1. Recruiter Screen
2. Hiring Manager Screen or a EM Screen
3. Program Management interview

5. System Design or Tech Depth interview
6. Collaboration with Engineers interview 
7. Leadership interview with a peer.

8. Culture fit with HRBP
9. hiring manager deep dive interview 
10. Skip level interview

If you pass through 7-10 you get an offer.

Here are the questions - I didn't include the standard stuff like tell me a bit about yourself, pointed questions at my background, why you are interested in the role, etc.

Round 1: Manager of PM
- Talk about domain, what that looks like at netflix, how the teams and products are structured, what is implemented, where the challenges are
- Share a time you worked with a stakeholder and couldn't give them what they wanted when they wanted it?
- Share a time you used data to make a decision, going back, is there anything you would have done differently?
- What do you think about netflix's latest culture memo? 

Round 2: SWE Manager
- How do you handle friction with engineering teams?
- If you had to move over every single org, team, and 3rd party at netflix to a new technology infrastructure (redacted, domain specific), how would you do it? How would you prioritize? How would you keep track of the risks? How would you iterate the plan as needs change?
- If you wanted to build something brand new, how would you continuously validate the success of the initiative? How would you articulate to engineering what needs to be done first and why?
- Share your experience in product-driven companies vs. engineering-driven companies?
